title: Biryani King Brings Punjabi Soul Food to Honolulu's Sheridan Street
excerpt: A Pakistani-born chef's home-style cooking — from charcoal tandoor naan to oxtail biryani — is winning over Hawaiʻi's food scene and its desi community.
body:
• Biryani King, a fast-casual Punjabi restaurant opened in May on Honolulu's Sheridan Street, serves home-style Pakistani Punjabi dishes made entirely from scratch
  • Owner-chef Shahnaz 'Mama' Hameed relocated from Virginia to Hawaiʻi, bringing recipes from Pakistan's Punjab province to a city with few South Asian dining options
  • The restaurant has drawn praise from Honolulu Magazine and the local desi community for its authentic biryanis, tandoor-baked breads and weekend brunch menu

In a small dining room off Sheridan Street, behind a Walmart and next to a vacant lot, Shahnaz Hameed rises at 4:30 each morning to begin the day's cooking. The aromas that fill Biryani King — cinnamon, cardamom, slow-braised meats — are drawing Honolulu diners to a style of food that has been largely absent from O'ahu's restaurant scene: home-style Punjabi cuisine from the heart of Pakistan.

Biryani King opened in May in the former space of a Thai restaurant, offering a cafeteria-style format where customers build plates from an array of daily entrees and sides. Hameed, who is of Indian descent from Pakistan's Punjab province, moved from Virginia to be closer to her son Zishan and his family — and to open the restaurant she had long envisioned.

Lahore Street Food, Island Style

"We chose to emulate the style of street food in Lahore," Zishan Hameed told Aloha State Daily. "If you go to Lahore, it's a food destination. Street food in Lahore is like Dotonburi in Osaka. You show up to a vendor and you eat it the way the chef makes it."

The menu rotates daily but anchors around biryani — the layered rice dish that gives the restaurant its name. Meat for the biryani is marinated in house-made yogurt and spices, with the protein alternating between chicken and goat. Honolulu Magazine's food critic called the biryanis "a revelation and the stars of the show," describing them as "impossibly fluffy" and "lifted by the heady perfume of cinnamon, cardamom, onions, ginger and other spices."

"She blends the spices herself; she makes the ghee herself. It's the most authentic, homestyle food you're going to have."

— Zishan Hameed, on his mother's cooking

Beyond biryani, the daily offerings include braised oxtail over basmati rice, butter chicken, daal tadka and chana masala. Everything is made from scratch — including charcoal tandoor-baked naan and roti, and lassis made with homemade yogurt. Plates range from $14.99 for vegetarian options to $19.99 for meat plates.

Filling a Gap in Hawaiʻi's Food Scene

The Hameed family sees their restaurant as filling a specific niche. Most Indian restaurants in Honolulu serve Nepali-influenced cuisine, which tends toward creamier, heavier preparations suited to mountainous climates. Punjabi cooking, shaped by the hot, flat geography of the Punjab region that straddles Pakistan and northwestern India, leans toward bolder spicing and meat-forward dishes including beef — a protein uncommon in Hindu-influenced Indian cooking.

"This is soul food, Punjabi food," Zishan said. "We put 'soul food from the heart of Punjab' as our slogan — because that's really what this food is. It's not Pakistani or Indian food; it's older than that."

A Weekend Brunch and Growing Following

The restaurant has introduced what Nikki Hameed, Zishan's wife, describes as the island's "first and only Punjabi-style breakfast." The Sunday brunch features samosas, chana chaat, pakora and halwa — a grain-based pudding cooked in ghee — served with puri, the airy deep-fried flatbread. The brunch menu was launched after repeated requests from Honolulu's Indian and Pakistani community.

Yelp reviews since the May opening have been overwhelmingly positive. "Been waiting for this food for years on island, finally it's here," wrote one reviewer. Another described both the lamb and oxtail as exceptionally tender, adding that owner Hameed "is definitely the Queen of her dishes."

A Diaspora Kitchen, 5,000 Miles From Punjab

For Honolulu's South Asian residents — and visiting members of the diaspora — Biryani King represents something that can be hard to find far from the subcontinent: food that tastes like home. Cards only, no cash. Open daily except Monday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. and 4 to 8 p.m., at 704 Sheridan Street.
